opus-5.5.text:
I see them as two pieces of the same larger picture rather than two separate products.

The way I'd put it is that Vision is about understanding the world: what's in the scene, what things are, how they relate to each other semantically. Depth is about the physical, geometric side: where things are, how far away, what shape they have in three-dimensional space. Humans do both at once without thinking about it. When you reach for a cup, you know it's a cup, and you also know exactly where it sits relative to your hand. For a machine, and especially for a robot, those two capabilities have historically been built quite separately, and that gap is one of the things holding embodied intelligence back.

So Depth, in a sense, is a very focused, very practical component. Real sensors are noisy. Depth cameras fail on transparent or reflective surfaces, on glass, on shiny metal, which is exactly the kind of thing a robot runs into in a kitchen or a factory. If your geometric perception is broken there, everything downstream, like grasping or navigation, falls apart. So we wanted something that gives reliable spatial perception you can actually put on a machine.

Vision is the broader foundation. It carries more of the general visual knowledge and representation learning, and ideally it's something many downstream tasks can build on.

The relationship is complementary, and over time I think they converge. My personal belief is that, in the long run, you don't want a semantic model and a geometric model stitched together with glue code. You want one representation of the world that natively understands both meaning and space. Releasing them as distinct pieces now is partly practical, since each solves a real problem people have today, and partly a step toward that more unified world model. For us, the end goal isn't any single model. It's giving robots perception good enough that they can actually act in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of them as two layers of the same thing, not two separate products.

Lingbo Vision is the foundation, the general visual world model. Its job is to understand and generate the visual world as a whole: how objects look, how they move, how light and geometry and physics behave over time. That's a very broad capability, and it's what we invest most of our research effort in.

Lingbo Depth is a more focused expression of that foundation. Depth, in a sense, is one of the most fundamental things a visual system has to understand, because almost everything downstream, whether it's 3D reconstruction, robotics, AR, or video generation that respects space, depends on knowing how far things are and how the scene is structured. So rather than treating depth as an isolated task, we treat it as a capability that falls out of a strong world model and then gets sharpened into something people can actually use today.

The relationship is bidirectional, though, and that's the part I find most interesting. The general model gives Depth its priors: a sense of what scenes typically look like, so it can handle hard cases like reflections, thin structures, or textureless regions. In return, pushing hard on depth forces the foundation model to get the geometry right, which makes its video understanding and generation more physically consistent. So Depth isn't just a downstream product. It's also a kind of diagnostic and training signal for Vision.

If I had to summarize it: Vision is where we build the understanding, and Depth is where we prove that understanding is real and deliver it to people in a concrete form. Over time I expect the boundary between them to blur, because a good world model shouldn't need a separate depth head at all. It should simply know.
